scenario.name: VMware/Broadcom, CISA AA23-039A & Mandiant DFIR — ESXi /var/log/shell.log, hostd.log & VMDK Hypervisor Forensics
scenario.overview: Imagine a huge warehouse holding dozens of locked steel office pods stacked on one master concrete foundation. An intruder logs into the warehouse basement console with stolen superintendent keys, pulls the emergency power cord on every running office pod so their steel floor bolts spring open, and runs a high-speed partial padlocking tool across every pod shell while three separate basement logbooks quietly record every command, every shutdown, and every tampered descriptor. In this scenario (T1078, VMware/Broadcom, CISA AA23-039A & Mandiant DFIR, ESXi /var/log/shell.log, hostd.log & VMDK Hypervisor Forensics), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: eSXi SSH Authentication, then mass Virtual Machine Termination via esxcli, then intermittent VMDK Encryption. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering ESXi SSH Authentication, then Mass Virtual Machine Termination via esxcli, then Intermittent VMDK Encryption, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates process, authentication, and network telemetry for T1078 across the documented kill chain.

stages.title: Stage 2: Mass Virtual Machine Termination via esxcli vm process kill (/var/log/hostd.log)
stages.subtitle: Impact (T1529 - System Shutdown/Reboot: Hypervisor VM Termination)
stages.description: Because every live office pod clamps down heavy locks on its own floor foundation while running, the intruder walks down the breaker panel flipping every pod off hard so every foundation slab pops unlocked simultaneously. Because running vmx hypervisor processes hold exclusive file locks on guest virtual disks (-flat.vmdk), the actor iterates through every World ID and runs esxcli vm process kill --type=force --world-id=<ID>. Both /var/log/shell.log and the VMware Host Agent log (/var/log/hostd.log) record the forced power-off of each guest VM (logged in Linux Audit Event 500 with EsxiLogFiles=/var/log/shell.log + /var/log/hostd.log, TerminatedWorldId=2104892 , Guest VM: CORP-DC01, KillType=--type=force , Immediate vmx termination to release VMDK locks so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). stages.title: Stage 3: Intermittent VMDK Encryption & Flat Descriptor Reconstruction (CISA ESXiArgs Recovery)
stages.subtitle: Impact (T1486 - Data Encrypted for Impact: VMFS Datastore VMDKs)
stages.description: Launching a portable padlocking press out of a temporary basement closet, the intruder races across the datastore locking slices of every virtual disk, configuration card, and memory file, leaving forensic responders to audit the footprint and check whether skipped disk slices allow recovery. The actor launches an ELF encryptor from /tmp/ targeting /vmfs/volumes/*/*/*.vmdk.vmx, and .nvram. As documented in CISA’s ESXiArgs recovery guidance, many hypervisor encryptors fully encrypt the small text descriptor (.vmdk) while only intermittently encrypting blocks of the multi-hundred-gigabyte raw data file (-flat.vmdk), allowing DFIR teams to recreate the .vmdk descriptor via vmkfstools -c and boot or mount the guest NTFS/ext4 partitions (logged in Linux Audit Event 59 with DatastorePath=/vmfs/volumes/datastore1/CORP-DC01/, TargetedFiles=*.vmdk, *-flat.vmdk, *.vmx, *.nvram, *.vswp, PreventiveKernelControl=esxcli system settings kernel set -s execInstalledOnly -v TRUE so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes Targeted Datastore Path: /vmfs/volumes/datastore1/CORP-DC01/CORP-DC01-flat.vmdk (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , Targeted Datastore Path: /vmfs/volumes/datastore1/CORP-DC01/CORP-DC01-flat.vmdk via System / so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1486 during "Intermittent VMDK Encryption & Flat Descriptor Reconstruction , CISA ESXiArgs Recovery" , The actor launches an ELF encryptor from /tmp/ targeting /vmfs/volumes/*/*/* while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact CISA Descriptor Recovery: ls -l *-flat.vmdk -> vmkfstools -c <exact_byte_size> -d thin temp.vmdk -> point Extent description to original -flat.vmdk runs (which executes VMware ESXi hypervisor management commands , CISA Descriptor Recovery: ls -l *-flat.vmdk -> vmkfstools -c <exact_byte_size> -d thin temp.v so that releases exclusive hypervisor locks on Guest VM flat disk files , *-flat.vmdk, *.nvram · T1486 during "Intermittent VMDK Encryption & Flat Descriptor Reconstruction , CISA ESXiArgs Recovery" so the ransomware encryptor can overwrite virtual disks at high speed, leaving audit trails in /var/log/shell.log and /var/log/hostd.log). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ /var/log/shell.log: nohup /tmp/encrypt /vmfs/volumes/datastore1/CORP-DC01/CORP-DC01-flat.vmdk / ⇠#3 ACK 59) from Node ③ (#3 ESXi Shell & /var/log/shell.log) to Node ④ (#4 hostd & esxcli vm process kill), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 /vmfs/volumes/* (-flat.vmdk)).

steps.plainTitle: Intermittent VMDK Encryption & Flat Descriptor Reconstruction (CISA ESXiArgs Recovery)
steps.storyAnalogy: Launching a portable padlocking press out of a temporary basement closet, the intruder races across the datastore locking slices of every virtual disk, configuration card, and memory file, leaving forensic responders to audit the footprint and check whether skipped disk slices allow recovery.
steps.simpleExplanation: The actor launches an ELF encryptor from /tmp/ targeting /vmfs/volumes/*/*/*.vmdk.vmx, and .nvram. As documented in CISA’s ESXiArgs recovery guidance, many hypervisor encryptors fully encrypt the small text descriptor (.vmdk) while only intermittently encrypting blocks of the multi-hundred-gigabyte raw data file (-flat.vmdk), allowing DFIR teams to recreate the .vmdk descriptor via vmkfstools -c and boot or mount the guest NTFS/ext4 partitions (logged in Linux Audit Event 59 with DatastorePath=/vmfs/volumes/datastore1/CORP-DC01/, TargetedFiles=*.vmdk, *-flat.vmdk, *.vmx, *.nvram, *.vswp, PreventiveKernelControl=esxcli system settings kernel set -s execInstalledOnly -v TRUE so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact).
